title: Add omarchy-diagnose-suspend-wake
author: ganjeez
body:
## Summary
- Adds `bin/omarchy-diagnose-suspend-wake`, a CLI that finds which device is waking the machine early from suspend and offers a persistent fix.
- Relates to #1635: that thread has several people independently hand-diagnosing USB/Bluetooth devices that keep pulling their machine out of suspend (one report needed a second, different device disabled on top of the first fix). This automates the diagnostic process instead of trial-and-error guessing.

## How it works
- `status` — lists every device currently allowed to wake the machine (read-only, no root needed).
- `test [seconds]` — requests N seconds of real S3 suspend via the RTC alarm (`rtcwake -m mem -s N`) and reports whether it actually held that long. A device that wakes the machine early does so within seconds, well short of the requested duration.
- `diagnose [seconds]` — confirms the problem reproduces, disables every wake-enabled device as a control, confirms *that* holds sleep, then re-enables candidates one at a time until it's found every culprit (deliberately sequential rather than binary search — binary search only finds one culprit when there may be several, and a sequential pass costs about the same number of suspend cycles as a real candidate list has in practice). Offers to write a udev rule for whatever it finds.
- `restore` — undoes whatever a `diagnose` run left disabled, without touching anything that was off by firmware default to begin with (tracked via a state file, so it can't guess wrong).

## Testing
Built and validated this after using the same manual technique (`rtcwake` timing + sequential bisection over `/proc/acpi/wakeup` and per-USB-device `power/wakeup`) to actually find and fix a real instance of this bug — a MacBookPro11,4 whose internal Bluetooth controller was waking it from suspend all night, draining a full battery in 6-7 hours instead of holding sleep. Details and the confirmed device ID are in [my comment on #1635](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/issues/1635#issuecomment-5674712503). Fixed with an overnight test after applying the equivalent of what `diagnose` now automates.

On top of that:
- `bash -n` clean, no syntax errors.
- `status` run against real hardware — correctly enumerates ACPI and USB wake-enabled candidates, correctly excludes a device already governed by an existing udev rule.
- The udev-rule-writing path verified via `udevadm test` in simulation mode against the real device — matches and writes the expected `power/wakeup: disabled`.
- `restore` and the interrupt trap verified not to touch devices that are disabled by firmware default (only ever act on the tool's own state-file-tracked set).

The full automated `diagnose` suspend-cycle loop itself hasn't been run end-to-end by me in this PR (it repeatedly suspends the machine it runs on, which isn't something to do unattended) — the manual walkthrough that validated the underlying approach is linked above, and the code paths it exercises are covered by the checks listed.

## Notes for maintainers
- No existing `CONTRIBUTING.md` or CI lint workflow found in the repo to match against — happy to adjust style/conventions if there's something I missed.
- Open to feedback on whether this should be wired into a menu/help surface beyond the `# omarchy:summary=/group=/args=` header convention used by other `bin/` scripts.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_018BTLCq2L5R78o78UtZ4pcb

@@ -0,0 +1,375 @@
+#!/bin/bash
+
+# omarchy:summary=Find which device wakes the machine early from suspend and offer a fix
+# omarchy:group=system
+# omarchy:args=<status|test|diagnose|restore> [seconds]
+
+# A machine that "sleeps" but drains its battery in hours instead of days is
+# usually not failing to suspend at all - it's being woken again and again by
+# a device that's allowed to signal a wake (Bluetooth heartbeats, a dock, a
+# stray PCIe root port) and never gets a chance to hold real S3 sleep. That
+# looks identical to a battery/firmware problem from the outside, so this
+# tool proves the difference: request N seconds of real sleep via the RTC
+# alarm and see whether the machine actually held it.
+#
+# The bisection re-enables one wake source at a time from a known-good
+# (everything disabled) baseline rather than binary-searching the candidate
+# list. Binary search is faster but only correct when exactly one culprit
+# exists; real machines showed up in the field with more than one (see
+# omacom/omarchy#1635), and a sequential pass finds all of them for the same
+# order of magnitude of suspend cycles that a real candidate list ever has.
+
+set -uo pipefail
+
+SECONDS_DEFAULT=60
+SETTLE_SECONDS=5 # pause between suspend cycles so drivers (esp. wifi) fully
+                  # come back up before the next one - see the diagnose loop
+ACPI_WAKEUP=/proc/acpi/wakeup
+STATE_FILE="${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/omarchy-diagnose-suspend-wake.state"
+RULE_FILE=/etc/udev/rules.d/91-omarchy-diagnosed-wake.rules
+
+# Never touched: without this the machine would have no way to wake at all
+# once every device-level wake source is disabled for the control test.
+ESSENTIAL_ACPI="LID0"
+
+require_root() {
+  if [[ $EUID -ne 0 ]]; then
+    echo "omarchy-diagnose-suspend-wake: needs root (rtcwake and the wakeup" \
+      "attributes under /sys and /proc both require it). Re-run with sudo." >&2
+    exit 1
+  fi
+}
+
+require_rtcwake() {
+  command -v rtcwake >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
+    echo "omarchy-diagnose-suspend-wake: rtcwake not found (package: util-linux)" >&2
+    exit 1
+  }
+}
+
+# --- device enumeration -----------------------------------------------------
+
+# name, kind, sysfs-node columns for every /proc/acpi/wakeup device currently
+# enabled, other than the essential one above. Some rows have no fourth
+# (sysfs node) column at all - those are left with an empty node field.
+acpi_enabled_candidates() {
+  awk -v essential="$ESSENTIAL_ACPI" '
+    NR > 1 && $1 != essential && $3 == "*enabled" {
+      node = (NF >= 4) ? $NF : ""
+      print $1 "\t" "acpi" "\t" node
+    }
+  ' "$ACPI_WAKEUP"
+}
+
+acpi_is_enabled() {
+  awk -v n="$1" 'NR > 1 && $1 == n { print ($3 == "*enabled") ? "enabled" : "disabled" }' "$ACPI_WAKEUP"
+}
+
+acpi_set() {
+  local name=$1 want=$2
+  [[ "$(acpi_is_enabled "$name")" == "$want" ]] && return 0
+  echo "$name" >"$ACPI_WAKEUP" 2>/dev/null
+}
+
+# bus-port id and sysfs path for every USB device (not hub) that's currently
+# wake-enabled - these sit a level below the ACPI toggle above (e.g. a
+# Bluetooth controller enumerates as its own USB device on the XHC1
+# controller's bus, and only its own attribute needs to change).
+usb_enabled_candidates() {
+  local dir attr
+  for dir in /sys/bus/usb/devices/*/; do
+    [[ -f "${dir}idVendor" ]] || continue # skip hubs/root controllers
+    attr="${dir}power/wakeup"
+    [[ -r $attr ]] || continue
+    [[ $(<"$attr") == "enabled" ]] || continue
+    printf '%s\tusb\t%s\n' "$(basename "$dir")" "$dir"
+  done
+}
+
+usb_set() {
+  local dir=$1 want=$2
+  echo "$want" >"${dir}power/wakeup" 2>/dev/null
+}
+
+all_candidates() {
+  acpi_enabled_candidates
+  usb_enabled_candidates
+}
+
+set_candidate() {
+  local name=$1 kind=$2 node=$3 want=$4
+  case $kind in
+    acpi) acpi_set "$name" "$want" ;;
+    usb) usb_set "$node" "$want" ;;
+  esac
+}
+
+# --- state file (interrupt/undo safety net) -----------------------------------
+#
+# Tracks exactly what THIS tool has disabled and not yet made permanent, so
+# `restore` (and the INT/TERM trap) can put things back precisely rather than
+# guessing from current state - some devices are disabled by firmware default
+# and must never be touched, so "re-enable everything that's off" is wrong.
+
+save_state() {
+  : >"$STATE_FILE"
+  printf '%s\n' "$@" >"$STATE_FILE"
+}
+
+clear_state() {
+  rm -f "$STATE_FILE"
+}
+
+# --- reporting ---------------------------------------------------------------
+
+describe_candidate() {
+  local name=$1 kind=$2 node=$3
+  case $kind in
+    usb)
+      local vendor product maker label
+      vendor=$(<"${node}idVendor") product=$(<"${node}idProduct")
+      maker=$(<"${node}manufacturer" 2>/dev/null); maker=${maker:-unknown vendor}
+      label=$(<"${node}product" 2>/dev/null); label=${label:-unnamed device}
+      printf '%s (USB %s:%s, %s %s)' "$name" "$vendor" "$product" "$maker" "$label"
+      ;;
+    acpi)
+      printf '%s (%s)' "$name" "${node:-no sysfs node}"
+      ;;
+  esac
+}
+
+suggest_rule() {
+  local name=$1 kind=$2 node=$3
+  case $kind in
+    usb)
+      local vendor product
+      vendor=$(<"${node}idVendor") product=$(<"${node}idProduct")
+      printf 'SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="%s", ATTR{idProduct}=="%s", ATTR{power/wakeup}="disabled"\n' \
+        "$vendor" "$product"
+      ;;
+    acpi)
+      local pci_addr=${node#pci:}
+      if [[ $pci_addr != "$node" && -e "/sys/bus/pci/devices/$pci_addr" ]]; then
+        printf 'SUBSYSTEM=="pci", KERNEL=="%s", ATTR{power/wakeup}="disabled"\n' "$pci_addr"
+      else
+        printf '# %s has no stable udev match this tool knows how to generate;\n' "$name"
+        printf '# re-run: echo %s | sudo tee %s   after every boot instead.\n' "$name" "$ACPI_WAKEUP"
+      fi
+      ;;
+  esac
+}
+
+# --- the actual sleep test ---------------------------------------------------
+
+# Prints "held" or "woke-early" on stdout; the elapsed seconds go to stderr
+# for the caller to log if it wants them. A device that's really going to
+# wake the machine early does so within a few seconds, so the pass threshold
+# only needs to allow for rtcwake's own suspend/resume transition overhead -
+# scaled down for short test durations rather than a flat 15s that would
+# swallow most of a 30s test.
+run_test() {
+  local seconds=$1 start end elapsed slack threshold
+  slack=$((seconds / 4))
+  ((slack > 15)) && slack=15
+  threshold=$((seconds - slack))
+
+  start=$(date +%s)
+  if ! rtcwake -m mem -s "$seconds" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    echo "rtcwake failed - can't tell whether this held sleep or not" >&2
+    echo "inconclusive"
+    return 1
+  fi
+  end=$(date +%s)
+  elapsed=$((end - start))
+  echo "elapsed: ${elapsed}s (requested ${seconds}s, threshold ${threshold}s)" >&2
+
+  if ((elapsed >= threshold)); then
+    echo "held"
+  else
+    echo "woke-early"
+  fi
+}
+
+# Several suspend/resume transitions back to back, with no gap between them,
+# has been observed to wedge a wifi chip's firmware interface badly enough
+# that only a reboot clears it (brcmfmac on Broadcom parts; likely not the
+# only affected driver) - independent of which wake sources are enabled or
+# disabled. A short pause after each resume gives drivers time to fully
+# settle before the next suspend starts, which is cheap insurance against
+# that even though it can't guarantee avoiding it on fragile hardware.
+settle() {
+  sleep "$SETTLE_SECONDS"
+}
+
+# --- subcommands --------------------------------------------------------------
+
+cmd_status() {
+  echo "Wake-enabled devices (candidates for a spurious wake):"
+  local any=0 name kind node
+  while IFS=$'\t' read -r name kind node; do
+    any=1
+    echo "  - $(describe_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node")"
+  done < <(all_candidates)
+  ((any)) || echo "  (none - only $ESSENTIAL_ACPI is enabled)"
+}
+
+cmd_test() {
+  local seconds=${1:-$SECONDS_DEFAULT}
+  echo "Suspending for ${seconds}s via RTC alarm..."
+  local result
+  result=$(run_test "$seconds")
+  case $result in
+    held) echo "Held the full duration - suspend is behaving normally." ;;
+    woke-early) echo "Woke up early - something is pulling this machine out of sleep. Run 'diagnose' to find it." ;;
+    *) echo "Could not complete the test." ;;
+  esac
+}
+
+# Re-enables exactly what this tool disabled and hasn't made permanent yet,
+# per the state file. Safe to run any time; a no-op if nothing is pending.
+cmd_restore() {
+  if [[ ! -s $STATE_FILE ]]; then
+    echo "Nothing pending - no wake sources were left disabled by this tool."
+    clear_state
+    return 0
+  fi
+  local name kind node
+  while IFS=$'\t' read -r name kind node; do
+    [[ -z ${name:-} ]] && continue
+    set_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node" enabled
+    echo "  re-enabled: $(describe_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node")"
+  done <"$STATE_FILE"
+  clear_state
+  echo "Restored."
+}
+
+trap 'echo; echo "Interrupted - restoring wake sources before exiting." >&2; cmd_restore >&2' INT TERM
+
+cmd_diagnose() {
+  local seconds=${1:-$SECONDS_DEFAULT}
+  mapfile -t candidates < <(all_candidates)
+
+  if [[ ${#candidates[@]} -eq 0 ]]; then
+    echo "Nothing but $ESSENTIAL_ACPI is wake-enabled already - no candidates to test."
+    return 0
+  fi
+
+  echo "This will suspend the machine repeatedly (up to $((${#candidates[@]} + 2)) times," \
+    "~${seconds}s each, ${SETTLE_SECONDS}s apart) to isolate which device wakes it early." \
+    "Save your work first. On some hardware, many suspend cycles in a row can leave a" \
+    "wifi/USB driver wedged until the next reboot (independent of anything this tool" \
+    "changes) - if networking looks broken afterward, that's the likely cause."
+  read -r -p "Continue? [y/N] " reply
+  [[ $reply =~ ^[Yy]$ ]] || { echo "Aborted."; return 1; }
+
+  echo "==> Baseline: does sleep hold at all right now?"
+  local baseline
+  baseline=$(run_test "$seconds")
+  settle
+  if [[ $baseline == "held" ]]; then
+    echo "Held cleanly - no spurious wake detected. Nothing to fix."
+    return 0
+  elif [[ $baseline != "woke-early" ]]; then
+    echo "Test was inconclusive; stopping without changing anything."
+    return 1
+  fi
+  echo "Confirmed: woke up early. Disabling every wake-enabled device to isolate the cause..."
+
+  save_state "${candidates[@]}"
+  local name kind node entry
+  for entry in "${candidates[@]}"; do
+    IFS=$'\t' read -r name kind node <<<"$entry"
+    set_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node" disabled
+  done
+
+  echo "==> Control: does sleep hold with everything disabled?"
+  local control
+  control=$(run_test "$seconds")
+  settle
+  if [[ $control != "held" ]]; then
+    echo "Still woke early even with every known wake source off. The cause isn't" \
+      "in this candidate list (could be EC/firmware-level) - restoring and stopping."
+    cmd_restore
+    return 1
+  fi
+
+  echo "Confirmed the fix is somewhere in this list. Re-enabling one at a time..."
+  local culprits=()
+  for entry in "${candidates[@]}"; do
+    IFS=$'\t' read -r name kind node <<<"$entry"
+    echo "==> Testing: $(describe_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node")"
+    set_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node" enabled
+    local result
+    result=$(run_test "$seconds")
+    settle
+    if [[ $result == "woke-early" ]]; then
+      echo "    culprit - disabling it again and keeping it off."
+      set_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node" disabled
+      culprits+=("$entry")
+    else
+      echo "    not the cause - leaving it enabled."
+    fi
+  done
+
+  if [[ ${#culprits[@]} -eq 0 ]]; then
+    echo "No single device reproduced it on re-enable (the earlier failure may have" \
+      "been intermittent). Nothing left disabled."
+    clear_state
+    return 0
+  fi
+
+  echo
+  echo "Found ${#culprits[@]} wake source(s) causing the early wake:"
+  local rule_lines=()
+  for entry in "${culprits[@]}"; do
+    IFS=$'\t' read -r name kind node <<<"$entry"
+    echo "  - $(describe_candidate "$name" "$kind" "$node")"
+    rule_lines+=("$(suggest_rule "$name" "$kind" "$node")")
+  done
+
+  echo
+  echo "Suggested udev rule ($RULE_FILE):"
+  printf '%s\n' "${rule_lines[@]}"
+  echo
+  read -r -p "Write this rule now so it survives a reboot? [y/N] " reply
+  if [[ $reply =~ ^[Yy]$ ]]; then
+    printf '%s\n' "${rule_lines[@]}" >"$RULE_FILE"
+    udevadm control --reload
+    clear_state # now governed by the rule; live state already matches it
+    echo "Wrote $RULE_FILE and reloaded udev."
+  else
+    save_state "${culprits[@]}"
+    echo "Left it disabled for this session only - it'll reset on reboot." \
+      "Run 'omarchy-diagnose-suspend-wake restore' to undo, or 'diagnose' again later."
+  fi
+}
+
+# --- entry point ---------------------------------------------------------------
+
+require_rtcwake
+
+case "${1:-}" in
+  status)
+    cmd_status
+    ;;
+  test)
+    require_root
+    cmd_test "${2:-}"
+    ;;
+  diagnose)
+    require_root
+    cmd_diagnose "${2:-}"
+    ;;
+  restore)
+    require_root
+    cmd_restore
+    ;;
+  *)
+    echo "Usage: omarchy-diagnose-suspend-wake <status|test|diagnose|restore> [seconds]" >&2
+    echo "  status    - list devices currently allowed to wake the machine from sleep"
+    echo "  test      - suspend for [seconds] (default $SECONDS_DEFAULT) and report whether it held"
+    echo "  diagnose  - find which device wakes it early and offer a persistent fix"
+    echo "  restore   - re-enable whatever this tool left disabled"
+    exit 2
+    ;;
+esac

comments.body:
Ran this end-to-end on the same MacBookPro11,4 from #1635 (negative-path with the fix already applied, and positive-path after temporarily re-enabling Bluetooth wake live to give it a real culprit to find again). Journal-verified: 10 real suspend cycles executed correctly (baseline, control-with-everything-disabled, then all 8 candidates tested one at a time), and the wake-toggle logic behaved exactly as designed throughout - each non-culprit device was correctly left re-enabled at the end.

One real finding from that run, now fixed in the latest commit: doing that many suspend/resume cycles back to back with no gap wedged the wifi driver (`brcmfmac`) badly enough that only a reboot cleared it - continuous `Timeout on response for query command` errors, NetworkManager toggling the radio couldn't recover it. This was independent of which wake sources were enabled/disabled at the time; it's a driver fragility under rapid cycling, not a bug in the toggle logic. Added a short settle pause between cycles and an upfront warning about the risk so it reads as a known hardware quirk rather than something the tool broke.

Also worth noting as a real limitation rather than something I've "fixed": that same run didn't reproduce the Bluetooth culprit on re-enable (all 8 candidates held), even though it's a confirmed, repeatable cause on this machine per the original issue comment. Best guess is BT's connection-supervision wake only fires when there's actually active traffic with the paired peripheral at that moment, so a single ~60s isolation window can miss it - a device's wake capability being "enabled" doesn't guarantee its intermittent trigger fires inside any given test window. `diagnose` already messages this ("the earlier failure may have been intermittent") and re-running catches it, but flagging here in case it's worth a more definitive fix (e.g. a longer default window, or multiple re-enable attempts per candidate before ruling it out) rather than just the current messaging.
